One of these springs is placed in each corner of a horizontal square plate. The axis of each
spring is in a vertical direction. These four springs support a total load of 160 N.
What is the total elastic potential energy stored in the four springs?
A
0.048 J
B
0.19 J
C
0.38 J
D
0.77 J

hints: Notice the $160 \text{ N}$ total load is shared equally by four identical vertical springs, so first work out the force on one spring.
Read the change in length in $\text{mm}$ from the straight-line force against change in length graph for that single-spring force, then convert to $\text{m}$.
Recall elastic energy is the area under the force-extension line, $0.5Fx$, for one spring and then multiply by four.
walkthrough: The four identical springs share the $160 \text{ N}$ load equally, so force on one spring is $F = 160/4 = 40 \text{ N}$.
Use the graph of force in $\text{N}$ against change in length in $\text{mm}$. At $F = 40 \text{ N}$ the line gives $x \approx 2.4 \text{ mm} = 0.0024 \text{ m}$.
Elastic potential energy is the area under the linear graph: $E = 0.5Fx$.
For four springs, $E_{total} = 4 \times 0.048 = 0.192 \text{ J}$, about $0.19 \text{ J}$. This is option B.

A.explanation: This is the energy in one spring only, $0.5 \times 40 \times 0.0024$, and misses the factor of four springs.

B.explanation: Each spring carries $40 \text{ N}$, compresses about $2.4 \text{ mm}$, and four times $0.5Fx$ gives about $0.19 \text{ J}$.

C.explanation: This is twice too large because it uses $Fx$ per spring instead of $0.5Fx$ for the triangular area under the force-extension graph.

D.explanation: This is the energy if a single spring carried the full $160 \text{ N}$ load with about $9.6 \text{ mm}$ compression, not shared between four springs.
